source: 復次，如先所說作及增長業，若先所說由五因緣成極重業，名定受業。與此相違，名不定受業。復有四業。一、異熟定，二、時分定，三、二俱定，四、二俱不定。諸阿羅漢所有不善決定受業，或於前生所作，或於此生先異生位所作，由少輕苦之所逼惱，便名果報已熟。若已轉依，果報種子皆永斷故，一切不受。所以者何？由佛世尊依未解脫相續，建立定受業故。
A: Furthermore, as previously stated regarding action (karman) that is performed and accumulated, if, as previously stated, it becomes extremely heavy due to five causes and conditions, it is called action that is certainly to be experienced (niyatavedanīya-karman). What is contrary to this is called action that is not certainly to be experienced (aniyatavedanīya-karman). There are also four [other] kinds of action: first, certainty of ripening (vipāka-niyata); second, certainty of time (kāla-niyata); third, certainty of both; and fourth, uncertainty of both. Regarding all unwholesome action that is certainly to be experienced possessed by an arhat (arhat)—whether performed in a previous life or performed in this life while still in the state of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana)—it is said that the fruit (vipāka) has ripened when they are afflicted by a small and light suffering. If they have already attained the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), because the seeds (bīja) of the fruit are forever severed, they do not experience any of it. For what reason? Because the Buddha, the Blessed One, established [the doctrine of] action that is certainly to be experienced in reliance upon the continuum (saṃtāna) of those who are not yet liberated.
B: Furthermore, as previously stated regarding action (karman) that is performed and accumulated, if, as previously stated, it becomes extremely heavy due to five causes and conditions, it is called action that is certainly to be experienced (niyatavedanīya-karman). What is contrary to this is called action that is not certainly to be experienced (aniyatavedanīya-karman). There are also four [other] kinds of action: first, certainty of ripening (vipāka-niyata); second, certainty of time (kāla-niyata); third, certainty of both; and fourth, uncertainty of both. Regarding all the unwholesome action that is certainly to be experienced possessed by an Arhant (arhant)—whether performed in a previous life or performed in this life while previously in the state of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana)—it is called "ripened fruit" (vipāka-phala) when they are afflicted by a small, light suffering. If they have already attained transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), because the seeds (bīja) of the fruit are all eternally severed, they do not experience any of it. For what reason? Because the Buddha Bhagavant (buddha bhagavant) established action that is certainly to be experienced based upon a continuum (saṃtāna) that is not yet liberated (vimukta).

source: 云何菩薩具於善行？此何行相？謂諸菩薩，於內成熟諸佛法故，於外成熟諸有情故，修行善行，是故說名具於善行。當知此行有七行相。一者、無所依止而惠施故；二者、無所依止而持戒故；三者、由哀愍心而修忍故；四者、非於少分修精進故；五者、為作利益諸有情處修靜慮故；六者、見不相應修妙慧故；七者、成熟方便善巧故。
A: How does a bodhisattva (bodhisattva) possess good practice (kuśala-dharma)? What is the nature of this practice? It is because bodhisattvas cultivate good practice in order to mature all Buddha-dharmas (buddha-dharma) internally and to mature all sentient beings (sattva) externally; therefore, it is said that they possess good practice. One should know that this practice has seven aspects: first, giving without any support (āśraya); second, observing morality (śīla) without any support; third, cultivating patience (kṣānti) out of a compassionate heart; fourth, cultivating vigor (vīrya) not merely in a small measure; fifth, cultivating meditative absorption (dhyāna) for the sake of benefiting sentient beings; sixth, cultivating profound wisdom (prajñā) by seeing what is not associated (viprayuj); and seventh, the maturity of skill in means (upāya-kauśalya).
B: How does a bodhisattva (bodhisattva) possess good practice (kuśaladharma-caryā)? What is the nature of this practice? It is because bodhisattvas cultivate good practice in order to mature the Buddha-dharmas (buddhadharma) internally and to mature sentient beings (sattva) externally; therefore, they are said to possess good practice. One should know that this practice has seven aspects: first, giving (dāna) without any reliance; second, maintaining morality (śīla) without any reliance; third, cultivating patience (kṣānti) out of a heart of compassion (karuṇā); fourth, cultivating vigor (vīrya) not just in a small measure; fifth, cultivating meditative absorption (dhyāna) for the sake of benefiting sentient beings; sixth, cultivating transcendent wisdom (prajñā) by seeing that which is not corresponding; and seventh, the skill in means (upāya-kauśalya) of maturation.

source: 云何菩薩清淨靜慮？謂此靜慮略有十種。一者、由世間淨，離諸愛味清淨靜慮。二者、由出世淨，無有染污清淨靜慮。三者、由加行淨，清淨靜慮。四者、由得根本淨，清淨靜慮。五者、由根本勝進淨，清淨靜慮。六者、由入、住、出自在淨，清淨靜慮。七者、捨靜慮已，復還證入自在淨，清淨靜慮。八者、神通變現自在淨，清淨靜慮。九者、離一切見趣淨，清淨靜慮。十者、一切煩惱、所知障淨，清淨靜慮。
A: What is the pure meditative absorption (dhyāna) of a bodhisattva? In brief, this meditative absorption is of ten kinds. First, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of the worldly (loka), being free from all craving for its flavor. Second, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of the supramundane (lokottara), being without any defilement (kliṣṭa). Third, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of the preparatory practice (prayoga). Fourth, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of attaining the fundamental (mūla). Fifth, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of the superior progress from the fundamental. Sixth, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of mastery in entering, abiding, and emerging. Seventh, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of mastery in abandoning the meditative absorption and then returning to realize and enter it again. Eighth, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of mastery in the miraculous manifestation of supernormal powers (abhijñā). Ninth, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of being free from all views (sarva-dṛṣṭi). Tenth, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of the purification of all defilements (sarva-kleśa) and the obstruction to knowledge (jñāna-āvaraṇa-viśuddhi).
B: What is the pure meditative absorption (dhyāna) of a bodhisattva? In brief, this meditative absorption is of ten kinds. First, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of worldly purity, being free from all craving for its flavor. Second, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of supramundane purity, being without any defilement. Third, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of the purity of preparatory practice (prayoga). Fourth, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of the purity of attaining the fundamental (maula). Fifth, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of the purity of superior progress from the fundamental. Sixth, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of the purity of mastery in entering, abiding, and emerging. Seventh, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of the purity of mastery in emerging from the meditative absorption and then returning to realize and enter it again. Eighth, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of the purity of mastery in the manifestation of supernormal powers (abhijñā). Ninth, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of being free from all inclinations toward views (dṛṣṭi). Tenth, the pure meditative absorption that is pure by way of the purity from all afflictions (kleśa) and the obstructions to knowledge (jñeyāvaraṇa).

source: 佛言：「如是！如是！須菩提！不可說義無增無減。菩薩摩訶薩習行般若波羅蜜，有方便力故，不作是念：『我增般若波羅蜜，乃至增檀波羅蜜。』當作是念：『但名字故，名檀波羅蜜。』是菩薩摩訶薩行檀波羅蜜時，是心及善根，如阿耨多羅三藐三菩提相迴向；乃至行般若波羅蜜時，是心及善根，如阿耨多羅三藐三菩提相迴向。」
A: The Buddha said: "So it is! So it is, Subhūti! The inexpressible meaning is without increase and without decrease. When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (great being) practices the Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), because of the power of skillful means (upāya), he does not think: 'I increase the Perfection of Wisdom, or even increase the Perfection of Giving (dānapāramitā).' He should think: 'It is only because of a name that it is called the Perfection of Giving.' When this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Perfection of Giving, he directs this mind and these roots of merit toward the characteristics of Unsurpassed Perfect Awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi); and even when practicing the Perfection of Wisdom, he directs this mind and these roots of merit toward the characteristics of Unsurpassed Perfect Awakening."
B: The Buddha said: "So it is, Subhūti! So it is! The meaning of the inexpressible (anabhilāpya) is neither increased nor decreased. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva (bodhisattva mahāsattva) trains in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), because of the power of skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), he does not think: 'I increase the perfection of wisdom, and so on, up to increasing the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā).' He should think: 'It is only because of a name (nāman) that it is called the perfection of giving.' When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving, he directs (pariṇāmay) this mind and these roots of goodness (kuśala-mūla) toward the aspect of supreme perfect enlightenment (samyaksambodhi); and so on, up to when he practices the perfection of wisdom, he directs this mind and these roots of goodness toward the aspect of supreme perfect enlightenment."

source: 佛告須菩提：「若菩薩摩訶薩如是知一切法性自離、一切法性自空，非聲聞、辟支佛作，亦非佛作；諸法相常住、法相、法住、法位、如、實際，是名菩薩行般若波羅蜜不離薩婆若念。何以故？般若波羅蜜性自離、性自空，不增不減故。」
A: The Buddha said to Subhūti, "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva (great being) thus knows that the nature of all dharmas (phenomena) is inherently detached and that the nature of all dharmas is inherently empty—not created by a śrāvaka (disciple), not created by a pratyekabuddha (solitary buddha), and also not created by a Buddha—and that the characteristics of all dharmas are eternally abiding (nitya), the dharma-lakṣaṇa (characteristic of phenomena), the dharma-sthiti (abiding of phenomena), the dharma-niyāmatā (fixed position of phenomena), suchness, and the reality-limit, this is called the bodhisattva-caryā (bodhisattva practice) of the prajñāpāramitā (perfection of wisdom) without departing from the sarva-ākārajña (omniscience) mindfulness. Why is this? Because the nature of the prajñāpāramitā is inherently detached and inherently empty, for it neither increases nor decreases."
B: The Buddha said to Subhūti: "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva (great being) thus knows that the nature of all phenomena (dharma) is inherently detached and that the nature of all phenomena is inherently empty, not created by a voice-hearer (śrāvaka) nor by a solitary buddha (pratyekabuddha), and also not created by a buddha; if he knows that the characteristics of all phenomena are eternally abiding, the dharma-characteristic (dharmalakṣaṇa), the dharma-abiding (dharmasthiti), the dharma-position (dharmaniyāma), suchness (tathatā), and the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), this is called the bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) without departing from the thought of omniscience (sarvajñatā). Why is this? Because the nature of the perfection of wisdom is inherently detached and inherently empty, for it neither increases nor decreases."

source: 復於所餘不同分界不現見蘊，比度觀察。謂彼所有，有為、有漏，遍一切處、遍一切種，於一切時，皆有如是法、皆墮如是理、皆有如是性。彼所有滅，皆永寂靜，常住安樂。彼所有道，皆能永斷，究竟出離。
A: Furthermore, regarding the remaining aggregates (skandha) that are not manifest in different realms, one should observe them through inference. It is said that whatever is conditioned (saṃskṛta) and tainted (sāsrava) is, in every place, in every mode, and at all times, possessed of such a nature, subject to such a principle, and characterized by such a quality. Whatever cessation (nirodha) there is for them is forever tranquil, permanently abiding, and blissful. Whatever path (mārga) there is for them is capable of forever cutting off and leads to ultimate departure.
B: Furthermore, regarding the remaining aggregates (skandha) that are not of the same category (sabhāga) and are not directly perceived (pratyakṣa), one should observe them through inference. That is to say, whatever is conditioned (saṃskṛta) and tainted (āsrava) among them, in all places (sarvatra) and in all modes (sarva-ākāra), at all times, all possess such phenomena, all fall under such principles, and all possess such a nature. Whatever cessation (nirodha) they possess is forever tranquil, permanently abiding (nitya), and blissful (sukha). Whatever path (mārga) they possess is capable of forever abandoning (prahāṇa) and is the ultimate (niṣṭhā) departure.

source: 「復次，聚落主！有受欲樂者，以法求財，不以濫取，以樂自供，供養父母，給足兄弟、妻子、奴婢、眷屬、知識，隨時供養沙門、婆羅門，仰求勝處安樂果報，未來生天，是名第三受欲樂者。
A: "Furthermore, village headman! There is one who enjoys sensual pleasures (kāma-bhoga) who seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma (dharma), not by illicit means, and uses that wealth to provide for his own happiness, to support his parents, to provide for his brothers, wife, children, servants, dependents, and acquaintances, and to make offerings at the proper times to ascetics (śramaṇa) and priests (brāhmaṇa), looking upward to a superior place and a fruit of happiness, and to birth in heaven in the future; this is called the third type of one who enjoys sensual pleasures."
B: "Furthermore, village headman, there is the one who experiences the pleasures of desire who seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma (dharma), not by improper means. With that wealth, he provides for his own happiness, makes offerings (pūjā) to his parents, and provides for his brothers, wife and children (putra-dāra), servants, attendants (parivāra), and friends (mitra). He makes offerings at the proper times to ascetics (śramaṇa) and brahmins (brāhmaṇa), looking upward to a superior state, a fruit of happiness (sukha), and a future (anāgata) birth in heaven. This is called the third type of person who experiences the pleasures of desire."

source: 又諸行中，無常、無恒、無不變易。此諸行中，常、恒、不變無性，非有為攝、非無為攝，共相觀識非不緣此境界而轉。若緣此境識不轉者，便於諸行常、恒、不變無性之中，不能如實智慧觀察。若不觀察，應不生厭；若不生厭，應不離欲；若不離欲，應無解脫；若無解脫，應無永盡究竟涅槃。若有此理，一切有情應皆究竟隨逐雜染，無出離期。是名第四言論道理。
A: Furthermore, among all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), there is impermanence (anitya), lack of constancy, and lack of immutability. Within these conditioned phenomena, the nature of permanence, constancy, and immutability is non-existent; they are neither included in the compounded (saṃskṛta) nor included in the uncompounded (asaṃskṛta). The consciousness that observes their common characteristics does not turn away from taking this domain (viṣaya) as its object. If the consciousness were not to turn toward this domain, then one would be unable to observe, with wisdom (prajñā) as it truly is (yathābhūtam), the non-existence of permanence, constancy, and immutability within all conditioned phenomena. If one does not observe this, one should not experience revulsion; if one does not experience revulsion, one should not become dispassionate; if one does not become dispassionate, there should be no liberation (vimukti); if there is no liberation, there should be no ultimate (niṣṭhā) and final nirvana (nirvāṇa). If this logic (yukti) were the case, all sentient beings (sarva-sattva) would necessarily follow defilement forever, with no time for departure. This is called the fourth principle of discourse.
B: Furthermore, among all compounded phenomena (saṃskāra), there is impermanence, instability, and change. Within these compounded phenomena, the nature of permanence, stability, and immutability is non-existent; it is not included among the compounded (saṃskṛta), nor is it included among the uncompounded (asaṃskṛta). The consciousness that observes the common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) does not turn without taking this state of affairs as its object. If, by taking this object, consciousness were not to turn, then one would be unable to observe according to reality (yathābhūta) with wisdom (prajñā) the non-existence of permanence, stability, and immutability within all compounded phenomena. If one does not observe, one should not experience revulsion (nirveda); if one does not experience revulsion, one should not become dispassionate (virāga); if one does not become dispassionate, one should not attain liberation (vimukti); if one does not attain liberation, one should not attain the ultimate, eternal cessation, which is nirvana (nirvāṇa). If this principle were true, all sentient beings (sattva) would ultimately remain subject to defilement (saṃkleśa) forever, with no time for emergence. This is called the fourth principle of discourse (yukti).

source: 「舍利弗！置閻浮提滿中如舍利弗、目連等。若滿三千大千世界如舍利弗、目連等；復置是事，若滿十方如恒河沙等世界如舍利弗、目連等智慧，欲比菩薩行般若波羅蜜智慧，百分不及一，千分百千分乃至算數譬喻所不能及。」
A: "Śāriputra, set aside the Jambudvīpa (Jambudvīpa) filled with beings like Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. If you were to fill the entire tri-sāhasra-mahat-sāhasra-lokadhātu (tri-sāhasra-mahat-sāhasra-lokadhātu) with beings like Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, and furthermore, set aside that matter and fill the ten directions (daśan-diś) with world systems (lokadhātu) as numerous as the sands of the Ganges (gaṅgā-nadī-vālikā) with beings possessing the wisdom (jñāna) of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, and if one wished to compare this to the wisdom of a bodhisattva (bodhisattva) practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), it would not reach a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor could it be reached by any calculation (gaṇanā) or analogy (upamā)."
B: "Śāriputra! Set aside the whole of Jambudvīpa filled with beings like Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. If you were to fill the entire great trichiliocosm (trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu) with beings like Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; and furthermore, set aside that matter, and if you were to fill world systems in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, with the wisdom of beings like Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, and wished to compare it to the wisdom of a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), it would not reach a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousandth part, or even any part reachable by calculation or analogy."

source: 佛告須菩提：「菩薩摩訶薩念般若波羅蜜，如般若波羅蜜中說，行是道，一念頃超越劫數，亦如彼人一日一夜心念之數。是菩薩摩訶薩行般若波羅蜜，遠離眾罪，所謂離阿耨多羅三藐三菩提罪。是菩薩摩訶薩行般若波羅蜜，一日所得善根功德，假令滿如恒河沙等三千大千世界中餘功德，猶亦不減；於餘殘功德，百分不及一分，千分千億萬分，乃至算數譬喻所不能及。」
A: The Buddha said to Subhūti: "A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (great being) who contemplates the Prajñāpāramitā (perfection of wisdom), as it is taught within the Prajñāpāramitā, and who practices this path, transcends the count of aeons in a single moment of thought, just as a person might count the thoughts of a single day and night. This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, remains far from all transgressions, which is to say, he remains far from the transgression of failing to attain the Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi (unsurpassed complete awakening). When this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, the Kuśala-mūla (wholesome roots) and Guṇa (merit) obtained in a single day are such that, even if one were to fill the Tri-sāhasra-mahat-sāhasra-lokadhātu (three-thousand-great-thousand world systems) with other merits, his merit would not be diminished; compared to those remaining merits, they do not reach even one part in a hundred, nor one in a thousand, a hundred thousand, or ten million, and they cannot be reached by any calculation or analogy."
B: The Buddha said to Subhūti, "A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (great being) who contemplates the Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), as it is taught within the Perfection of Wisdom, and who practices this path, transcends the count of eons in a single moment of thought, just as a person might count the thoughts of a day and a night. This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, practicing the Perfection of Wisdom, remains far from all transgressions, which is to say, he remains far from the transgression of failing to attain Unsurpassed Perfect Awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). When this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Perfection of Wisdom, the roots of merit (kuśalamūla) and virtues (puṇya) obtained in a single day are such that, even if one were to fill the three-thousand-great-thousand-fold world systems with other virtues equal to the sands of the Ganges, they would not diminish; compared to these remaining virtues, those others do not reach even one part in a hundred, nor one in a thousand, a hundred thousand, or ten million, and they cannot be reached by any calculation or analogy."

source: 「舍利弗！置閻浮提滿中如舍利弗、目連等。若滿三千大千世界如舍利弗、目連等；復置是事，若滿十方如恒河沙等世界如舍利弗、目連等智慧，欲比菩薩行般若波羅蜜智慧，百分不及一，千分百千分乃至算數譬喻所不能及。」
A: "Śāriputra! Set aside the whole of Jambudvīpa filled with beings like Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. If you were to fill the entire great trichiliocosm (trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu) with beings like Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; and furthermore, set aside that matter, and if you were to fill world systems in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, with the wisdom of beings like Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, and wished to compare it to the wisdom of a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), it would not reach a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousandth part, or even any part reachable by calculation or analogy."
B: "Śāriputra! Set aside the whole of Jambudvīpa filled with beings like Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.

source: 佛告舍利弗：「若彼比丘諂曲幻偽、欺誑、不信、無慚無愧、懈怠失念、不定惡慧、慢緩、違於遠離、不敬戒律、不顧沙門行、不求涅槃、為命出家。如是比丘不應教授，與共言語。所以者何？此等比丘破梵行故。若彼比丘不諂曲、不幻偽、不欺誑、信心、慚愧、精勤正念、正定智慧、不慢緩、心存遠離、深敬戒律、顧沙門行、志崇涅槃、為法出家。如是比丘應當教授。所以者何？如是比丘能修梵行，能自建立故。」
A: The Buddha said to Śāriputra: “If a bhikṣu is devious, deceitful, fraudulent, faithless, lacking in shame and moral dread, lazy, lacking in mindfulness (smṛti), unstable, of evil wisdom (prajñā), sluggish, averse to seclusion, disrespectful of the precepts (śikṣāpada), unconcerned with the conduct of a śramaṇa, and does not seek nirvāṇa, but has gone forth (pravrajyā) for the sake of his livelihood—such a bhikṣu should not be instructed or spoken with. For what reason? Because such bhikṣus destroy the holy life (brahmacarya). If a bhikṣu is not devious, not deceitful, not fraudulent, possesses faith, possesses shame and moral dread, is diligent, possesses mindfulness, possesses correct concentration and wisdom, is not sluggish, keeps his mind set on seclusion, deeply respects the precepts, is concerned with the conduct of a śramaṇa, aspires to nirvāṇa, and has gone forth for the sake of the Dharma—such a bhikṣu should be instructed. For what reason? Because such a bhikṣu is able to cultivate the holy life and is able to establish (pratiṣṭhā) himself.”
B: The Buddha said to Śāriputra: "If that monk is devious, deceitful, fraudulent, untrusting, lacking in shame (hrī) and lacking in remorse (apatrāpya), lazy, lacking in mindfulness (smṛti), lacking in stable wisdom (prajñā), sluggish, opposed to seclusion (viveka), disrespectful of the training rules (śikṣāpada), unmindful of the conduct of a renunciant (śramaṇa), and does not seek liberation (nirvāṇa), having gone forth for the sake of his livelihood, such a monk should not be instructed or spoken with. For what reason? Because such monks destroy the holy life (brahmacarya). If that monk is not devious, not deceitful, not fraudulent, is trusting, possesses shame and remorse, is diligent and mindful, possesses stable wisdom, is not sluggish, keeps his mind set on seclusion, deeply respects the training rules, is mindful of the conduct of a renunciant, aspires to liberation, and has gone forth for the sake of the Dharma, such a monk should be instructed. For what reason? Because such a monk is able to cultivate the holy life and is able to establish himself."

source: 復次，建立極微，當知有五種勝利。謂由分析一合聚色安立方便，於所緣境便能清淨廣大修習，是初勝利。又能漸斷薩迦耶見，是第二勝利。如能漸斷薩迦耶見，如是亦能漸斷憍慢，是第三勝利。又能漸伏諸煩惱纏，是第四勝利。又能速疾除遣諸相，是第五勝利。如是等類，應當如理思惟極微。
A: Furthermore, in establishing the subtle atom (paramāṇu), one should know there are five kinds of advantages (anuśaṃsa). By means of the method (upāya) of analyzing the composite form, one is able to practice purely and extensively upon the object of perception (ālambana); this is the first advantage. Furthermore, one is able to gradually abandon the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi); this is the second advantage. Just as one is able to gradually abandon the view of a self-existent body, so too is one able to gradually abandon arrogance (māna); this is the third advantage. Furthermore, one is able to gradually subdue all the fetters of the defilements (kleśa); this is the fourth advantage. Furthermore, one is able to quickly dispel all marks (nimitta); this is the fifth advantage. Regarding such matters as these, one should reflect appropriately (yoniśomanasikāra).
B: Furthermore, regarding the establishment of the subtle atom (paramāṇu), one should know there are five kinds of advantages. By means of the method of analyzing the composite form (rūpa), one is able to practice purely and extensively upon the object of perception (ālambana); this is the first advantage. Furthermore, one is able to gradually sever the view of self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi); this is the second advantage. Just as one is able to gradually sever the view of self-identity, so too is one able to gradually sever arrogance (māna); this is the third advantage. Furthermore, one is able to gradually subdue all the fetters of defilement (kleśaparyavasthāna); this is the fourth advantage. Furthermore, one is able to quickly dispel all marks (nimitta); this is the fifth advantage. In this way and others, one should contemplate the subtle atom according to reality.

source: 論曰：善無漏法亦名為妙。諸染污法亦名有罪有覆及劣。准此妙劣，餘中已成，故頌不辯。諸有為善亦名應習，餘非應習義准已成。何故無為不名應習？不可數習令增長故。又習為果，此無果故。解脫涅槃亦名無上，以無一法能勝涅槃，是善是常超眾法故。餘法有上，義准已成。
A: The treatise says: Virtuous (kuśala) undefiled (anāsrava) phenomena (dharma) are also called excellent (praṇīta). All defiled (saṃkliṣṭa) phenomena are also called faulty (sāvādya), obstructive (āvṛta), and inferior (hīna). Based on these categories of excellent and inferior, the status of the remainder is already established by implication, and therefore the verse does not discuss it. All conditioned (saṃskṛta) virtuous phenomena are also called worthy of cultivation (bhāvanīya), and the fact that others are not worthy of cultivation is established by implication. Why is the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) not called worthy of cultivation? Because it cannot be repeatedly cultivated to cause it to increase. Furthermore, cultivation has a result, and this has no result. Liberation (vimukti) and Nirvana (nirvāṇa) are also called supreme (anuttara), because there is no phenomenon that can surpass Nirvana, as it is virtuous, eternal (nitya), and transcends all phenomena. That other phenomena have something superior to them is established by implication.
B: The treatise says: Virtuous undefiled phenomena (anāsrava-dharma) are also called excellent (anuttara). All defiled phenomena (kliṣṭa) are also called faulty, covered, and inferior. Based on these categories of excellent and inferior, the status of the remainder is already established by implication, and therefore the verse does not discuss it. All virtuous conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) are also called worthy of cultivation; the remainder is not worthy of cultivation, which is established by implication. Why is the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) not called worthy of cultivation? Because it cannot be repeatedly cultivated to cause growth. Furthermore, cultivation has a result, and this has no result. Liberation (vimukti) and Nirvana (nirvāṇa) are also called supreme (anuttara), because there is not one phenomenon that can surpass Nirvana, as it is virtuous, eternal, and transcends all phenomena. The remainder of phenomena have something superior to them, which is established by implication.

source: 復次，云何菩薩失壞大乘？謂有菩薩，聞一切法甚深無性，即執一切煩惱燒然自性本無，謂已無有生死重病。譬如有人，於己身中所生熱病，謂為無病，於此熱病不能解脫，名為失壞。由此譬喻，失壞菩薩，當知亦爾。
A: Furthermore, how does a bodhisattva (bodhisattva) lose the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna)? It is when a bodhisattva hears that all phenomena (dharma) are profound and lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva), and immediately clings to the view that all defilements (kleśa) are burning and inherently non-existent, believing that the grave sickness of birth-and-death (saṃsāra) no longer exists. It is like a person who, having a fever within their own body, claims to be free of sickness; because they cannot be liberated from this fever, it is called a loss. By this analogy, you should know that a bodhisattva who has suffered such a loss is the same.
B: Furthermore, how does a bodhisattva (bodhisattva) lose the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna)? It is when a bodhisattva hears that all phenomena (sarva-dharma) are profound and without intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva), and immediately clings to the view that the burning intrinsic nature of all defilements (sarva-kleśa) is originally non-existent, claiming that the grave sickness of transmigration (saṃsāra) no longer exists. It is like a person who, having a fever within their own body (kāya), claims to be without sickness; because they cannot be liberated (vimukti) from this fever, it is called a loss. By this analogy, one should know that the bodhisattva who has suffered a loss is likewise.

source: 長者答言：「我之所見真實、有為、思量、緣起，若復真實、有為、思量、緣起者，彼則無常，無常者是苦。如是知已，於一切見都無所得。如汝所見：『世間常，此是真實，餘則虛妄。』者，此見真實、有為、思量、緣起；若真實、有為、思量、緣起者，是則無常，無常者是苦。是故汝等習近於苦，唯得於苦，堅住於苦，深入於苦。如是汝言世間無常，此是真實，餘則虛妄。有如是咎。」
A: The householder (gṛhapati) replied: “What I see is real (satya), conditioned (saṃskṛta), thought-constructed (cintā), and dependent-arising (pratītyasamutpāda). If it is real, conditioned, thought-constructed, and dependent-arising, then it is impermanent (anitya). What is impermanent is suffering (duḥkha). Having known it in this way, one attains no-apprehension (anupalambha) regarding all views (dṛṣṭi). As for your view that ‘the world (loka) is permanent, this is real, and the rest is false,’ this view is real, conditioned, thought-constructed, and dependent-arising. If it is real, conditioned, thought-constructed, and dependent-arising, then it is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. Therefore, you all associate with suffering, obtain only suffering, remain firmly in suffering, and sink deeply into suffering. In the same way, when you say ‘the world is impermanent, this is real, and the rest is false,’ there is this same fault.”
B: The elder replied: "What I see is real (satya), conditioned (saṃskṛta), thought-out (cintāmaya), and dependent-arising (pratītyasamutpanna). If it is real, conditioned, thought-out, and dependent-arising, then it is impermanent (anitya). What is impermanent is suffering (duḥkha). Having known this, one finds nothing to grasp in all views. As for your view that 'The world is eternal, this is real, and all else is false,' this view is real, conditioned, thought-out, and dependent-arising. If it is real, conditioned, thought-out, and dependent-arising, then it is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. Therefore, you all associate with suffering, obtain only suffering, remain firmly in suffering, and sink deep into suffering. Thus, when you say 'The world is impermanent, this is real, and all else is false,' you have such a fault."

source: 「是菩薩以天耳淨，過於人耳，聞二種聲：天聲、人聲。亦不著是天耳神通，天耳與聲及己身皆不可得，自性空故、自性離故、自性無生故。不作是念：『我有是天耳。』除為薩婆若心。如是，舍利弗！菩薩摩訶薩行般若波羅蜜時，得天耳神通智證。
A: "The bodhisattva, by means of the purity of the divine ear (divya-śrotra), surpassing that of humans, hears two kinds of sounds: divine sounds and human sounds. He does not become attached to this supernormal power (abhijñā) of the divine ear; the divine ear, the sounds, and his own body are all unattainable, because their self-nature (svabhāva) is empty (śūnyatā), because their self-nature is detached, and because their self-nature is non-arising (anutpāda). He does not form this thought: 'I possess this divine ear,' except for the sake of the mind of omniscience (sarva-ākārajña). Thus, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), he attains the realization of the supernormal knowledge (abhijñā-jñāna) of the divine ear."
B: "That bodhisattva (bodhisattva), with the purity of the divine ear (divyaśrotra), surpassing human hearing, hears two kinds of sounds: divine sounds and human sounds. He does not become attached to this supernormal power (abhijñā) of the divine ear; the divine ear, the sounds, and his own body are all unattainable, because their self-nature (svabhāva) is empty, because their self-nature is detached, and because their self-nature is non-arising. He does not entertain the thought: 'I possess this divine ear,' except for the sake of the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā). Thus, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva (mahāsattva) practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), he attains the realization of the wisdom of the supernormal power of the divine ear."

source: 爾時，須菩提及大眾歡喜讚歎般若波羅蜜，作是言：「大波羅蜜，所謂般若波羅蜜。」大波羅蜜者，所謂一切法雖自性空，而般若波羅蜜能利益菩薩，令得阿耨多羅三藐三菩提；雖得，亦無所得；雖轉法輪，亦無所轉。
A: At that time, Subhūti and the great assembly rejoiced and praised the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), saying: "The great perfection (mahāpāramitā), that is to say, the perfection of wisdom." The great perfection is that which, although all phenomena (dharma) are empty in their own-nature (svabhāva), the perfection of wisdom is able to benefit the bodhisattva, causing them to attain unsurpassed, perfect awakening (anuttarasamyaksambodhi); yet, although they attain it, there is no attainment; although they turn the wheel of the dharma (dharmacakra), there is no turning.
B: At that time, Subhūti and the great assembly rejoiced and praised the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), saying: "The great perfection, that is to say, the perfection of wisdom." The great perfection is that which, although all phenomena (sarva-dharma) are empty of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-śūnyatā), the perfection of wisdom is able to benefit the bodhisattva, enabling them to attain unsurpassed, perfect awakening (anuttarasamyaksambodhi); although they attain it, there is no attainment (anupalambha); although they turn the wheel of the dharma, there is nothing turned.

source: 答：若已與果種子相續，名過去界；若未與果，當來種子相續，名未來界；若未與果，現在種子相續，名現在界。當知此中如是密意。若苾芻等於如是種子相續中而得善巧，名於彼彼一切法中證得無量種種自性諸界善巧。
A: The answer is: If a continuum of seeds (bīja) has already produced a fruit (phala), it is called the past realm (atīta-dhātu); if it has not yet produced a fruit and the continuum of seeds is for the future, it is called the future realm (anāgata-dhātu); if it has not yet produced a fruit and the continuum of seeds is present, it is called the present realm (pratyutpanna-dhātu). You should know that this is the hidden intention (abhisandhi) here. If a monk (bhikṣu) attains skill (kauśalya) in such a continuum of seeds, he is said to have attained, in those various phenomena (sarva-dharma), skill in the immeasurable and various self-natures (svabhāva) of all realms.
B: The answer is: If a continuum of seeds (bīja) has already produced a fruit (phala), it is called the past realm (atīta-dhātu); if it has not yet produced a fruit, but the continuum of seeds is directed toward the future, it is called the future realm (anāgata-dhātu); if it has not yet produced a fruit, but the continuum of seeds is present, it is called the present realm (pratyutpanna-dhātu). You should understand the hidden meaning (abhisandhi) here in this way. If a monk (bhikṣu) or others attain skill (kauśalya) in such a continuum of seeds, they are said to have attained, in all these various phenomena (dharma), skill in the various realms (dhātu) of infinite and diverse natures (svabhāva).

source: 言無有餘福德如菩薩摩訶薩力勢者，是中自說因緣：「菩薩行般若時，得諸法平等忍；得平等忍故，雖行空，亦能生四無量心。」四無量心中，大悲是大乘之本；見眾生就於死法，如囚受戮。諸菩薩能生六波羅蜜等乃至一切種智，是故諸菩薩能生大悲。
A: Regarding the statement that there is no other merit equal to the power and influence of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, the cause and condition for this is explained therein: "When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), he attains the patience (kṣānti) of the equality of all phenomena (dharma). Because he attains this patience of equality, although he practices emptiness (śūnyatā), he is also able to give rise to the four immeasurables (apramāṇa). Among the four immeasurables, great compassion (mahākaruṇā) is the root of the great vehicle (mahāyāna); he sees sentient beings approaching the phenomena of death, like prisoners awaiting execution. Bodhisattvas are able to give rise to the six perfections (pāramitā) and so on, up to the omniscience of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā); it is for this reason that bodhisattvas are able to give rise to great compassion."
B: Regarding the statement that there is no other merit (puṇya) equal to the power and influence of a bodhisattva mahāsattva (bodhisattva mahāsattva), the reason is explained therein: "When a bodhisattva practices wisdom (prajñā), he attains the patience (kṣānti) of the equality of all phenomena (dharma); because he attains this patience of equality, although he practices emptiness (śūnyatā), he is also able to give rise to the four immeasurables (catur-apramāṇa)." Among the four immeasurables, great compassion (mahat-karuṇā) is the root of the great vehicle (mahāyāna); he sees beings approaching the law of death, like prisoners awaiting execution. All bodhisattvas are able to give rise to the six perfections (ṣaṣ-pāramitā) and so forth, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects (sarva-ākāra-jña); it is for this reason that all bodhisattvas are able to give rise to great compassion.

source: 佛言：「阿難！不如弟子以般若波羅蜜相應法為菩薩摩訶薩說，乃至一日，其福多！置一日，但半日；置半日，但一食頃；置一食頃，但須臾間說，其福多！何以故？菩薩摩訶薩善根勝一切聲聞、辟支佛故。菩薩摩訶薩自欲得阿耨多羅三藐三菩提，亦示、教、利、喜他人，令得阿耨多羅三藐三菩提。阿難！如是菩薩行六波羅蜜，行四念處乃至行一切種智，增益善根，若不得阿耨多羅三藐三菩提，無有是處！」
A: The Buddha said: "Ānanda, if a disciple were to teach a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (great being) the doctrine corresponding to the Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), even for a single day, the merit would be great. Setting aside a day, even for half a day; setting aside half a day, even for the duration of a single meal; setting aside the duration of a single meal, even for a brief moment of teaching, the merit would be great. Why is this? Because the wholesome roots (kuśala-mūla) of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva surpass those of all Hearers (śrāvaka) and Solitary Buddhas (pratyekabuddha). A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva desires to attain the Unsurpassed, Right and Perfect Enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) for himself, and he also demonstrates, instructs, benefits, and gladdens others, causing them to attain the Unsurpassed, Right and Perfect Enlightenment. Ānanda, in this way, a Bodhisattva practicing the six Perfections (pāramitā), practicing the four Establishments of Mindfulness (smṛti-upasthāna), and even practicing the Knowledge of All Aspects (sarva-ākārajña), increases his wholesome roots; that he should not attain the Unsurpassed, Right and Perfect Enlightenment is an impossibility."
B: The Buddha said: "Ānanda, if a disciple were to teach a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (great being) the doctrine corresponding to the Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) for even a single day, the merit would be great. Setting aside a day, even for half a day; setting aside half a day, even for the duration of a single meal; setting aside the duration of a single meal, even for a mere moment of teaching, the merit is great. Why is this? Because the wholesome roots (kuśalamūla) of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva surpass those of all Hearers (śrāvaka) and Solitary Buddhas (pratyekabuddha). A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva desires to attain Unsurpassed, Right and Perfect Enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) for himself, and he also demonstrates, instructs, benefits, and gladdens others, causing them to attain Unsurpassed, Right and Perfect Enlightenment. Ānanda, that a Bodhisattva who thus practices the six Perfections (pāramitā), practices the four Establishments of Mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), and even practices the Omniscience of all aspects (sarvajñatā), thereby increasing his wholesome roots, would not attain Unsurpassed, Right and Perfect Enlightenment—such a situation does not exist."
